column1: Basic, Standard, and Premium belong to Azure SQL Database's {{c1::DTU}} purchasing model.
column2:
The DTU model bundles CPU, memory, and I/O in predefined sizes. A tier change changes the available bundle. The vCore model exposes compute capacity more directly.
Review source

column1: Eligible SQL Server licenses can reduce provisioned General Purpose or Business Critical vCore costs through {{c1::Azure Hybrid Benefit}}.
column2:
Azure Hybrid Benefit applies eligible existing SQL Server licenses to reduce qualifying Azure costs. Serverless compute does not qualify, so do not factor that discount into a serverless estimate.
Review source
Review serverless limits

column1: In the standard Azure SQL Database Business Critical architecture, one primary is paired with {{c1::three secondary replicas}}.
column2:
Business Critical keeps secondary replicas available for failover. The readable secondary belongs to this group rather than being an extra replica beyond it. Read-only work can use its separate compute.
Review source

column1: A Hyperscale database supports {{c1::zero to four}} high-availability secondary replicas.
column2:
The primary is not part of this count. Additional high-availability secondaries can serve as failover targets, but they add compute cost. Named replicas for separately sized read workloads are a different choice.
Review source

column1: Serverless compute scaling stays between the configured {{c1::minimum and maximum vCores}}.
column2:
The minimum and maximum define how far serverless compute can scale down or up while active. The chosen range also affects available memory and I/O resources.
Review source

column1: In Azure SQL Database, serverless compute is supported in General Purpose and {{c1::Hyperscale}}.
column2:
General Purpose and Hyperscale offer serverless as a compute option. Selecting serverless is separate from selecting the service tier. Business Critical does not offer that compute option.
Review source

column1: The default MAXDOP for new Azure SQL databases since September 2020 is {{c1::8}}.
column2:
The default of 8 applies to newly created Azure SQL databases from the stated date. Existing databases retain their configured values, so inspect the actual configuration when investigating parallelism.
Review source

column1: To request serial query execution, set MAXDOP to {{c1::1}}.
column2:
MAXDOP 1 requests a serial plan for the relevant query or scope. It does not prevent other sessions from running queries at the same time.
Review source

column1: For one query, override database-level parallelism with {{c1::OPTION (MAXDOP 2)}} to request MAXDOP 2.
column2:
This hint changes the parallelism limit for the statement rather than the database. It does not require the optimizer to choose a parallel plan or guarantee that exactly two workers will run.
Review source

column1: Set the current database's MAXDOP to 4 with {{c1::ALTER DATABASE SCOPED CONFIGURATION SET MAXDOP = 4;}}
column2:
This command changes a setting for the current database, not the whole server. A separate FOR SECONDARY configuration can set the limit for secondary replicas.
Review source

column1: In Azure SQL Database, enable automatic index creation with {{c1::ALTER DATABASE CURRENT SET AUTOMATIC_TUNING (CREATE_INDEX = ON);}}
column2:
This command turns on automatic index creation for the current Azure SQL database. The service can assess the benefit of indexes it creates. The command does not explicitly change the other tuning options.
Review source

column1: As of November 2026, new Azure SQL databases default to compatibility level {{c1::170}}.
column2:
Compatibility level 170 is the documented default for new Azure SQL databases. An existing database retains its setting until it is changed. The default does not establish what every database currently uses.
Review source

column1: Compatibility level 150 or higher allows {{c1::batch mode on rowstore}} for eligible queries without columnstore indexes.
column2:
A rowstore stores data by row. Batch mode processes groups of rows at once and can benefit eligible queries even without a columnstore index. The compatibility level allows the feature but does not guarantee its use.
Review source

column1: At level 150 or higher, {{c1::table variable deferred compilation}} uses the table variable's actual row count at first execution.
column2:
The optimizer delays compilation until the table variable has its initial rows. It can then use that row count to choose a plan. Later executions can still reuse the plan made for the first count.
Review source

column1: At compatibility level 150 or higher, {{c1::scalar UDF inlining}} can substitute eligible user-defined function logic into the calling query.
column2:
A scalar user-defined function returns one value. Inlining substitutes eligible function logic into the calling query so the optimizer can plan it together with the surrounding statement.
Review source

column1: At level 160 or higher, {{c1::Parameter Sensitive Plan optimization}} handles parameterized queries that need different plans for different parameter values.
column2:
Parameter sensitivity occurs when different parameter values match very different amounts of data. PSP lets eligible queries have different cached plan variants instead of forcing every value to share one plan.
Review source

column1: At level 160 or higher, {{c1::cardinality estimation (CE) feedback}} improves estimation assumptions from repeated query execution.
column2:
Cardinality estimation predicts how many rows a query operation will process. Feedback uses repeated executions to choose assumptions that better fit the data. The compatibility level alone does not make every query eligible.
Review source

column1: At compatibility level 170, {{c1::optional parameter plan optimization (OPPO)}} can choose different plans for NULL and non-NULL optional filter values.
column2:
An optional filter can return all rows for NULL and a smaller group for a non-NULL input. OPPO can select different plans for those cases when the query and configuration qualify.
Review source

column1: Set the current Azure SQL database's compatibility level to 170 with {{c1::ALTER DATABASE CURRENT SET COMPATIBILITY_LEVEL = 170;}}
column2:
This command changes the current database's compatibility setting rather than upgrading the engine itself. Use a performance baseline to compare important queries before and after the change.
Review source

column1: Enable database-scoped ad hoc plan stubs with {{c1::ALTER DATABASE SCOPED CONFIGURATION SET OPTIMIZE_FOR_AD_HOC_WORKLOADS = ON;}}
column2:
This database setting stores a small stub when a new ad hoc batch first compiles. Repeated batches can still receive full cached plans. The purpose is to save cache memory, not to speed up every execution.
Review source
